a5149.t:
Tomorrow, Michael Sang Correa, a 45-year-old Gambian citizen and alleged former member of the notorious “Junglers” death squad, will learn his fate in a landmark US federal trial at the Alfred A. Arraj United States Courthouse in Denver. The jury has concluded deliberations in what marks the first prosecution of a non-US citizen under the US Torture Act for crimes committed abroad, a case watched closely by human rights advocates and Gambian activists worldwide.
Correa faces six counts of torture and one count of conspiracy to commit torture, stemming from his alleged role in brutalizing suspected coup plotters following a failed 2006 attempt to overthrow former Gambian President Yahya Jammeh.
Prosecutors allege that Correa and other Junglers subjected victims to severe physical and mental abuse, including beatings with pipes and wires, suffocation with plastic bags, electric shocks, and dripping molten plastic or acid on detainees’ bodies. The accusations detail a harrowing campaign of violence at Gambia’s Mile 2 Prison and National Intelligence Agency headquarters, targeting political opponents during Jammeh’s 22-year dictatorship, which ended in 2017.
The trial, which began on April 7, 2025, has been a significant test of universal jurisdiction, a legal principle allowing the prosecution of grave international crimes regardless of where they occurred or the nationality of the accused. Testimonies from survivors, including former Gambian military officer Pharing Sanyang and others who traveled to Denver, described enduring extreme cruelty at the hands of Correa and his unit.
Their accounts, corroborated by findings from Gambia’s Truth, Reconciliation, and Reparations Commission (TRRC), painted a grim picture of systematic torture under Jammeh’s regime.
Correa’s defense argued that he was a low-ranking private acting under duress, facing potential torture or death himself if he disobeyed orders.
Defense attorney Nicholas Westbroek emphasized to jurors that “following an order is not the same as agreeing,” highlighting the climate of fear within the Junglers. Prosecutors countered that Correa made deliberate choices, noting that some Junglers refused to participate despite the risks, urging the jury to hold him accountable for his actions.
The case has drawn international attention as a rare instance of the US leveraging its 1994 Torture Act. Only two prior prosecutions under the statute have involved US citizens.
A guilty verdict could see Correa facing up to 20 years per count, potentially totaling 140 years in prison. An acquittal, however, might lead to immigration proceedings, given his expired visa status, with possible deportation to Gambia or extradition for other alleged crimes, including extrajudicial killings linked to the Junglers.
Human rights organizations, such as the Center for Justice and Accountability (CJA), which represents victims in the case, have hailed the trial as a step toward justice for Jammeh’s victims. “This case sends a clear message: perpetrators of atrocities have nowhere to hide,” said CJA attorney Carmen Cheung Ka-Man.
In Gambia, activists like Fatoumata Sandeng, whose father died in detention, see the trial as a complement to ongoing efforts to establish a Special Tribunal for Jammeh-era crimes, approved by ECOWAS in December 2024.
As the verdict looms, the outcome will likely resonate far beyond Denver, shaping the global fight against impunity and offering a measure of closure—or continued anguish—for survivors of Gambia’s dark chapter. The court is set to reconvene tomorrow, April 15, 2025, to deliver the jury’s decision.

a5553.t:
A Swapo Party MP in the National Assembly, Tobie Aupindi, said the August House should unanimously call on the United States of America to lift the economic, financial, and commercial blockade against Cuba and its people.
Dr. Aupindi added that the Assembly also urges the U.S. to immediately remove Cuba from the list of alleged state sponsors of terrorism.
Last week, Aupindi tabled a motion in the National Assembly calling on the United States to lift the more than 60-year-old blockade against Cuba and for it to be removed from the list of states allegedly sponsoring terrorism.
Motivating the motion, Dr. Aupindi reminded MPs of the strong and historic ties between Namibia and Cuba, noting the sacrifices and support Cuba gave to Namibia during the struggle for independence.
At the same time, he pointed out that Namibia also enjoyed cooperation with the United States, particularly through programmes such as the President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), which provided vital health support.
But Aupindi said tensions between the U.S. and Cuba can be traced back to the Cold War era, underlined by the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1978.
"However, despite the Cold War ending some 34 years ago, the blockade on Cuba remains in place today. Today, some 63 years later, the blockade remains enforced, causing economic devastation in Cuba and great opportunities being missed by both the United States and Cuba. The current status quo is not sustainable for either country."
He stressed that the blockade caused catastrophic economic losses to the island nation.
Since its imposition, Cuba is estimated to have lost more than one trillion U.S. dollars in opportunities and growth, losses he described as unsustainable, especially for a small economy like Cuba.
Dr. Aupindi concluded by saying Namibia stands ready to offer its mediation and play a meaningful role in promoting lasting peace, coexistence and economic opportunities between the United States and Cuba.
Debate on the motion will resume on Tuesday after it was adjourned by the leader of the official opposition, Imms Nashinge.

a5560.t:
- The Teddy Bear Clinic, which forms part of the larger The Teddy Bear Foundation, is actively addressing financial challenges through creative fundraising initiatives, including luxury raffles, a trap cycling challenge, and a black-tie dinner.
- These efforts aim to combat child abuse, gender-based violence, and support vulnerable groups.
- Financial delays in Gauteng and high caseloads significantly impact the clinic's operations, but their mission to promote healing for children remains steadfast.
In a bid to continue their advocacy and support for victims of child abuse and gender-based violence (GBV), The Teddy Bear Clinic, which forms part of the larger The Teddy Bear Foundation, has launched a series of creative fundraising initiatives.
These efforts come at a time when non-governmental organisations (NGOs) like theirs are grappling with financial constraints, hindering their ability to meet the ever-growing demands for their services.
The financial struggles faced by NGOs globally and in South Africa have reached a crisis point, as Shaheda Omar, clinical director of The Teddy Bear Clinic, unveiled in a recent conversation with News24.
Omar highlighted the dire situation NGOs are navigating and the proactive initiatives her organisation is taking to continue supporting vulnerable children.
To combat the hurdles of insufficient funding, The Teddy Bear Clinic has launched a series of fundraising initiatives. One of the highlights is a luxury raffle offering a two-night stay at the Mdluli Safari Lodge and R10 000 worth of Frozen for You vouchers.
A minimum donation of R50 is required for entry. Additional events include a trap cycling challenge and a black-tie dinner at the Sanctuary Mandela Hotel in Houghton on 28 June. Those interested can find out more HERE.
"I think we in the NGO sector have been struggling for a long time. Unfortunately, it's not a new phenomenon, but it has become bleak. Look at the financial landscape, not only of South Africa but globally. We can see how the USAID funding has impacted so many service providers globally and, even in South Africa, where services have been shut down."
Omar lamented the dwindling resources and its impact on collaboration among civil society organisations, noting that the competition brewing among NGOs often resulted in secrecy and a lack of unity.
"Instead of us standing united, holding hands, and trying to work together, that's not what we are finding on the ground or in practice," she said.
She shared the heart-wrenching story of a young girl impregnated twice by a teacher, a case that underscores the necessity of the clinic's work.
"She ingested rat poison to terminate the first pregnancy and contracted HIV following the second. These are victims who are so helpless in their fight against the scourge inflicted on them."
With limited funding posing significant challenges, Omar stressed how it affects the clinic's operations and the well-being of its staff.
"We are overloaded. Caseloads are high, and the work comes at a price. It affects the human resources of the foundation, increasing stress levels and volumes, and there is always the risk of compassion fatigue and burnout," said.
Despite these challenges, The Teddy Bear Clinic remains undeterred and continues to raise awareness, provide education, and offer healing and support to children in crisis.
"Every rand makes a difference in the journey to healing a child. Our mission is about promoting healing, support, and providing these children with a voice," said Omar.
Gauteng NGO funding crisis
The Gauteng NGO funding crisis revolves around the delayed funding and subsidies for non-profit organisations (NPOs) in the Gauteng province. The Department of Social Development (DSD) has been criticised for its handling of the funding process, with NGOs taking the department to court over delays in funding and subsidies for two months.
In January, News24 reported that the Gauteng Care Crisis Committee (GCCC) approached the courts after the department failed to comply with court orders related to the funding of NPOs.
Months later, they are in court for delayed funding for these NPOs. This comes after the Gauteng High Court ordered the Gauteng Department of Social Development to pay NPOs in May 2024.
The court ordered the department to finalise funding applications for NPOs, issue service-level agreements, and pay NPOs within seven days of signing the agreements. Repeated non-compliance led to the crisis committee seeking further court action.
GCCC chairperson Lisa Vetten said there was a need for "accountability and transparency" regarding the funding decisions made by the department.
"The impact of funding delays on NGOs and their communities is severe, and it is urgent to resolve these issues to uphold socio-economic rights," she said.
Vetten said some organisations faced closure "with reports of suicides due to lack of services".
"There are firm deadlines to settle these outstanding issues as the end of the financial year approaches," Vetten said.

a5621.t:
La Nation Bénin...
Samedi 24 octobre dernier l’Organisation des Nations Unies (ONU) a soufflé ses 70 bougies. A l’occasion, de nombreuses personnalités politico-administratives se sont associées à l’équipe pays de l’institution au Bénin, pour le traditionnel vœu de bon et heureux anniversaire.
«A 70 ans, l’ONU peut faire un retour sur le fier bilan, celui d’avoir travaillé avec de nombreux partenaires pour éliminer le colonialisme, vaincre l’apartheid, maintenir la paix dans des lieux en proie à des troubles et formuler un ensemble de traités et de droits pour protéger les droits humains. Chaque jour, l’ONU nourrit des personnes souffrant de la faim, offre un abri aux refugiés et vaccine les enfants contre la poliomyélite et d’autres maladies mortelles. Nos travailleurs humanitaires bravent des environnements reculés et dangereux pour fournir l’aide humanitaire, et nos médiateurs s’efforcent de trouver un terrain d’entente entre les parties belligérantes et des solutions pacifiques aux griefs et aux différends». Ce morceau choisi du message du secrétaire général de l’ONU, Ban Ki-Moon, résume, à lui tout seul, l’importance de l’institution. C’est dire que si l’ONU n’avait pas existé, il aurait fallu la créer de toute urgence au vu des multiples crises que traverse le monde.
Selon le coordonateur résident du Système des Nations Unies au Bénin, Rosine Sori Coulibaly, cette institution est née des suites du chaos et des ravages de la seconde guerre mondiale. Elle ajoute que sa mission est restée toujours guidée par sa charte qui oriente ses interventions dans les domaines piliers de la paix, du développement durable et des droits de l’Homme. 
Au cours des manifestations officielles, à Cotonou, vendredi 23 octobre dernier, Rosine Sori Coulibaly a indiqué que l’ONU est aujourd’hui à un tournant de son histoire avec l’adoption, le 25 septembre dernier, du nouvel agenda de développement durable à l’horizon 2030 qui comprend 17 Objectifs de Développement durable (ODD) déclinés en 189 cibles.
«Depuis l’indépendance du Bénin, les Nations Unies ont appuyé le pays dans son processus de développement en fournissant une aide matérielle conséquente, mais aussi une assistance technique», a-t-elle déclaré. Elle poursuit que depuis 1990, de grands progrès, avec l’appui des Nations Unies et de l’ensemble des partenaires au développement, ont été faits. Ainsi, la parité des filles-garçons dans l’enseignement primaire est en passe d’être atteinte ; la polio a été éradiquée ; et enfin, la proportion de la population souffrant de la faim a été réduite de moitié.
Une bonne coopérations avec le Bénin
De la coopération avec le Bénin, le coordonnateur du SNU au Bénin relève que pour la période 2014-2018, les Nations Unies lui fourniront un appui financier et technique conséquent. Soit près de 970 millions de dollars US. «Au-delà de cette aide matérielle, nous mettons à disposition des institutions et du peuple béninois, nos expertises dans six domaines d’interventions : la croissance inclusive, l’emploi, la sécurité alimentaire, l’égalité du genre et protection sociale, la santé y compris le VIH/Sida, les maladies non transmissibles, la nutrition, la planification familiale, l’assainissement, de base, l’éducation de base, la protection contre la vulnérabilité sociale, les violences et les abus, la gouvernance, et la décentralisation et enfin l’environnement, la gestion des crises, catastrophes et les changements climatiques.
L’ensemble des agences résidentes et non résidentes opérant au Bénin s’emploie désormais à faire du Bénin un pays phare dans la mise en œuvre de la Réforme des Nations Unies dénommée «Unis dans l’action», a-t-elle souligné. 
«Cette réforme vise le renforcement de la cohérence et de la synergie des actions de l’organisation internationale afin de rationaliser les coûts tout en garantissant la qualité des interventions au bénéfice des populations», conclut Rosine Sori Coulibaly.
Au cours de cette même cérémonie, le ministre en charge des Affaires étrangères, Saliou Akadiri a d’abord souhaité bon anniversaire à l’institution et relevé que les 55 ans de présence de l’ONU au Bénin sont le signe de l’attachement de notre pays à ses valeurs. «C’est l’occasion pour réaffirmer les valeurs et succès de l’Organisation et rappeler les nombreux défis qui sont les siens», a-t-il ajouté.
Il a, par ailleurs, assuré l’institution de la disponibilité constante des services de l’administration béninoise pour l’accomplissement de sa mission.
La cérémonie a été l’occasion pour quatre de nos confrères, de recevoir leurs récompenses pour la qualité de leurs productions relatives aux Objectifs de Développement durable.
a5621.en:
La Nation Bénin...

Last Saturday, 24 October, the United Nations Organisation (UN) blew out its 70 candles. For the occasion, many political and administrative figures joined the institution's country team in Benin for the traditional wish of a good and happy anniversary.

"At 70, the UN can look back on a proud record, that of having worked with many partners to eliminate colonialism, defeat apartheid, maintain peace in troubled places and craft a body of treaties and rights to protect human rights. Every day, the UN feeds people suffering from hunger, shelters refugees and vaccinates children against polio and other deadly diseases. Our humanitarian workers brave remote and dangerous environments to deliver humanitarian aid, and our mediators strive to find common ground between warring parties and peaceful solutions to grievances and disputes." This selected passage from the message of the UN Secretary-General, Ban Ki-Moon, sums up on its own the importance of the institution. Which is to say that if the UN had not existed, it would have had to be created as a matter of urgency given the many crises the world is going through.

According to the Resident Coordinator of the United Nations System in Benin, Rosine Sori Coulibaly, this institution was born out of the chaos and devastation of the Second World War. She adds that its mission has always remained guided by its charter, which orients its interventions in the pillar areas of peace, sustainable development and human rights.

During the official ceremonies in Cotonou last Friday, 23 October, Rosine Sori Coulibaly stated that the UN is today at a turning point in its history with the adoption, on 25 September, of the new sustainable development agenda for 2030, which comprises 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) broken down into 189 targets.

"Since Benin's independence, the United Nations has supported the country in its development process by providing substantial material aid, but also technical assistance," she declared. She goes on to say that since 1990, great progress has been made with the support of the United Nations and of all development partners. Thus, gender parity between girls and boys in primary education is close to being achieved; polio has been eradicated; and finally, the proportion of the population suffering from hunger has been halved.

Good cooperation with Benin

On cooperation with Benin, the coordinator of the UN System in Benin notes that for the 2014-2018 period the United Nations will provide the country with substantial financial and technical support: nearly 970 million US dollars. "Beyond this material aid, we place at the disposal of Benin's institutions and people our expertise in six areas of intervention: inclusive growth, employment, food security, gender equality and social protection, health including HIV/AIDS, non-communicable diseases, nutrition, family planning, basic sanitation, basic education, protection against social vulnerability, violence and abuse, governance, and decentralisation, and finally the environment, the management of crises and disasters, and climate change."

All the resident and non-resident agencies operating in Benin are now working to make Benin a flagship country in the implementation of the United Nations reform known as "Delivering as One," she stressed.

"This reform aims to strengthen the coherence and synergy of the international organisation's actions in order to rationalise costs while guaranteeing the quality of interventions for the benefit of the people," Rosine Sori Coulibaly concludes.

During the same ceremony, the Minister in charge of Foreign Affairs, Saliou Akadiri, first wished the institution a happy anniversary and noted that the 55 years of UN presence in Benin are a sign of our country's attachment to its values. "It is an occasion to reaffirm the values and successes of the Organisation and to recall the many challenges it faces," he added.

He further assured the institution of the constant availability of the services of the Beninese administration for the accomplishment of its mission.

The ceremony was also an opportunity for four of our colleagues to receive their awards for the quality of their output relating to the Sustainable Development Goals.

a5657.t:
Dakar, 4 fév (APS) – La suspension de l’aide publique au développement annoncée par le président des États-Unis d’Amérique concerne un programme d’électrification mis en œuvre au Sénégal avec un financement de 318 milliards de francs CFA du gouvernement américain, a déclaré le Premier ministre sénégalais, Ousmane Sonko, lundi, à Fass Touré, dans la région de Louga (nord).
‘’Nous ne pouvons pas continuer à dépendre de l’aide étrangère. Avant-hier, le nouveau président américain a annoncé une suspension de tous les programmes d’aide au développement des États-Unis en faveur des pays pauvres, pour une durée de trois, en attendant de voir ce qu’il en fera’’, a dit M. Sonko en s’exprimant en wolof.
‘’L’un des financements suspendus était destiné à un programme d’électrification mis en œuvre au Sénégal. C’est un financement de 500 millions de dollars américains (318 milliards de francs CFA, selon le cours actuel du dollar)’’, a ajouté le Premier ministre dans un enregistrement diffusé par le site d’information Seneweb (privé).
Il a invité ses compatriotes à travailler dur pour ne plus dépendre de l’aide fournie par les pays développés. ‘’Doit-on continuer à dépendre de l’aide étrangère ? Nous devons travailler dur à la mise en œuvre de nos programmes. Si nous faisons cela, nous serons cités, dans les années à venir, parmi les pays les mieux gérés’’, a dit Ousmane Sonko.
L’initiative ‘’Sénégal Power Compact’’, dont la durée d’exécution est de cinq ans, est financé par le Millenium Challenge Corporation, un programme du gouvernement américain.
Ce projet d’électrification mis en œuvre au Sénégal depuis 2024 bénéficie d’un don de 550 millions de dollars des États-Unis d’Amérique et d’une contribution de 50 millions de dollars américains de l’État sénégalais.
Il est destiné à accroître la production d’énergie électrique du pays et à augmenter le nombre de Sénégalais ayant accès à l’électricité.
À Fass Touré, Ousmane Sonko présidait la cérémonie de lancement de la deuxième phase du Projet d’approvisionnement en eau potable en milieu rural, qui est financée avec 64 milliards de francs CFA de China Exim Bank, une banque publique chinoise.
Ces travaux d’adduction d’eau d’une durée de trente mois seront exécutés par la société chinoise CGCOC.
Il s’agit de construire 85 forages, 89 châteaux d’eau, un réseau de distribution d’eau de 1.450 kilomètres et 300 bornes fontaines.
Source: http://www.aps.sn
a5657.en:
SENEGAL-UNITED STATES-COOPERATION / Donald Trump has suspended an electrification project worth 318 billion CFA francs in Senegal, according to Ousmane Sonko

Dakar, 4 Feb (APS) – The suspension of official development assistance announced by the President of the United States of America concerns an electrification programme implemented in Senegal with 318 billion CFA francs of financing from the American government, Senegalese Prime Minister Ousmane Sonko declared on Monday at Fass Touré, in the Louga region (north).

“We cannot continue to depend on foreign aid. The day before yesterday, the new American president announced a suspension of all United States development aid programmes for poor countries, for a period of three [months], pending a decision on what he will do with them,” said Mr Sonko, speaking in Wolof.

“One of the suspended financings was destined for an electrification programme implemented in Senegal. It is a financing of 500 million US dollars (318 billion CFA francs at the current dollar exchange rate),” the Prime Minister added in a recording broadcast by the (private) news website Seneweb.

He invited his compatriots to work hard so as no longer to depend on aid provided by developed countries. “Should we continue to depend on foreign aid? We must work hard to implement our own programmes. If we do that, we will be cited, in the years to come, among the best-managed countries,” said Ousmane Sonko.

The “Senegal Power Compact” initiative, whose implementation period is five years, is financed by the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a programme of the American government.

This electrification project, implemented in Senegal since 2024, benefits from a grant of 550 million dollars from the United States of America and a contribution of 50 million US dollars from the Senegalese state.

It is intended to increase the country's electricity production and to increase the number of Senegalese with access to electricity.

At Fass Touré, Ousmane Sonko was presiding over the launch ceremony of the second phase of the Rural Drinking Water Supply Project, which is financed with 64 billion CFA francs from China Exim Bank, a Chinese public bank.

These water-supply works, lasting thirty months, will be carried out by the Chinese company CGCOC.

The plan is to build 85 boreholes, 89 water towers, a water distribution network of 1,450 kilometres and 300 standpipes.

Source: http://www.aps.sn

a5725.t:
Djibouti devient membre du Conseil d’administration du GPE pour un mandat de 3 ans, représentant les pays d’Afrique francophones aux côtés du Tchad. Depuis 2016, Djibouti a activement contribué aux différents comités techniques du GPE.
Du 4 au 7 juin 2024 à Berlin, en Allemagne, le ministre de l’Éducation Nationale et de la Formation Professionnelle, M. Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, accompagné par le Secrétaire Général du MENFOP, a participé aux travaux du Conseil d’administration du GPE.
Le Conseil d’administration du GPE, organe directeur suprême, définit les politiques et orientations stratégiques, supervise les finances, et évalue les résultats du GPE. Composé de 40 membres issus des pays en développement, bailleurs de fonds, sociétés civiles, secteur privé, fondations, organismes multilatéraux et banques régionales, il se réunit deux fois par an pour des décisions stratégiques.
Lors de cette mission, le ministre Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud a contribué substantiellement aux discussions sur les attributions de financements et la stratégie de financement du GPE pour 2025-2030. Il a également partagé les politiques éducatives de Djibouti définies par le Président Ismaïl Omar Guelleh et les résultats de l’école citoyenne, ainsi que les transformations en cours, notamment l’école rurale intégrée.
En marge des réunions, le ministre a participé à plusieurs panels sur les innovations et la mobilisation de financements pour une éducation de qualité inclusive. Il a été l’invité d’honneur de l’événement célébrant la Journée internationale du jeu, partageant l’expérience de Djibouti en matière d’éducation préscolaire fondée sur la pédagogie basée sur le jeu, soutenue par USAID Djibouti.
Egalement, le ministre de l’Éducation Nationale et de la Formation Professionnelle, Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, a eu l’occasion de rencontrer M. Jakaya Kikwete, président du Conseil d’administration du Partenariat Mondial pour l’Éducation et ancien Président de la République-Unie de Tanzanie (2005-2015), ainsi que Mme Laura Frigenti, Directrice générale du Partenariat mondial pour l’éducation. Ces rencontres ont permis d’échanger sur les perspectives et les défis du secteur éducatif en Afrique et dans le monde.
La participation active de Djibouti au sein du GPE et la mise en œuvre d’initiatives éducatives innovantes témoignent de son engagement ferme à offrir une éducation de qualité à tous ses apprenants.
A savoir que le GPE est le plus grand fonds au monde dédié exclusivement à transformer l’éducation dans les pays à faible revenu.
En tant que partenariat unique et multipartite, il travaille à offrir une éducation de qualité à tous les enfants afin qu’ils puissent bénéficier des opportunités qui en découlent.
Source : Menfop
a5725.en:
Djibouti becomes a member of the GPE Board of Directors for a three-year term, representing French-speaking African countries alongside Chad. Since 2016, Djibouti has actively contributed to the various technical committees of the GPE.

From 4 to 7 June 2024 in Berlin, Germany, the Minister of National Education and Vocational Training, Mr. Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, accompanied by the Secretary General of MENFOP, took part in the work of the GPE Board of Directors.

The GPE Board of Directors, the supreme governing body, defines policies and strategic orientations, oversees finances, and evaluates the GPE's results. Made up of 40 members drawn from developing countries, donors, civil society, the private sector, foundations, multilateral bodies and regional banks, it meets twice a year to take strategic decisions.

During this mission, Minister Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud contributed substantially to the discussions on funding allocations and on the GPE's financing strategy for 2025-2030. He also shared Djibouti's education policies as defined by President Ismail Omar Guelleh and the results of the "citizen school", as well as the transformations under way, notably the integrated rural school.

On the margins of the meetings, the minister took part in several panels on innovations and on mobilising financing for inclusive quality education. He was the guest of honour at the event celebrating the International Day of Play, sharing Djibouti's experience in pre-school education based on play-based pedagogy, supported by USAID Djibouti.

The Minister of National Education and Vocational Training, Moustapha Mohamed Mahamoud, also had the opportunity to meet Mr. Jakaya Kikwete, Chair of the Board of the Global Partnership for Education and former President of the United Republic of Tanzania (2005-2015), as well as Ms. Laura Frigenti, Chief Executive Officer of the Global Partnership for Education. These meetings made it possible to exchange views on the prospects and challenges of the education sector in Africa and in the world.

Djibouti's active participation within the GPE and the implementation of innovative educational initiatives bear witness to its firm commitment to offering quality education to all its learners.

It should be noted that the GPE is the largest fund in the world dedicated exclusively to transforming education in low-income countries.

As a unique multi-stakeholder partnership, it works to provide quality education to all children so that they may benefit from the opportunities that flow from it.

Source: Menfop

a5746.t:
MONROVIA – The United States government’s decision to pause foreign aid for 90 days has already had dire consequences across the global community, and Liberia is seemingly also feeling the pinch. Aware of the situation, Liberia’s House of Elders, the Senate, led by Grand Bassa County Senator Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, has been busy around the clock, figuring out a sane way out of the quagmire. In the last couple of days, the Senate continues to hold brainstorming meetings with the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, as well as other Ministries, Agencies and Commissions, to circumvent if not cure the impact of USAID suspension and its possible permanent cancel. The Analyst reports.
The Liberian Senate’s pursuit of solutions to the U.S. suspension of USAID and accompanying negative impact on the Liberian economy culminated into a meeting Monday, February 24, 2025, engaging sector ministries and agencies particularly affected by the action.
The Senate, through its Committees on Health, Agriculture, Education and Ways, Means, Finance and Budgeting brainstormed together with several the government ministries and agencies in an effort share notes on first-hand information about the impact of the USAID withdrawal and possible solution.
The ministries and agencies provided information to the Senate on the current status of the situation and their respective ideas for the way forward.
Prominent amongst them was the Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Mr. Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, who informed the Liberian Senate that the Ministry was analyzing and documenting how the USAID shutdown is impacting the country.
The Ministry, he said, was preparing for all eventualities beyond the three months which the US government indicated was the timeframe for the USAID suspension, costing Liberia $118 in loss.
The impact of the cut, Ngafuan said, affects several government institutions that include Health, Education, Elections, and Domestic revenue mobilization, prayerful that other projects may not be affected in the coming days or weeks.
From the interactions and engagements with the various sector ministries and agencies, the Liberian Senate also uncovered that the Architecture, Engineering, and Construction Oversight Services for Water and Health Infrastructure, which was valued at $2.9 million, and a community-led monitoring project worth $185,000 being implemented by an NGO, were all affected.
One of the largest affected programs is the Education System Strengthening Project, valued at $23.4 million, which aimed to enhance Liberia’s educational sector.
Other projects on the list include Elections and Democracy ($15.9 million) and Local Empowerment for Accountability and Decentralization (LEAD) ($17.9 million).
The Senate Committees’ public hearings on the analysis and way-forward on the impact of the cancellation of the USAID to Liberia is an outcome of the Senate plenary’s decision last Tuesday, February 4, 2025, asking the Committees on Ways, Means and Finance, Foreign Affairs, and Agriculture to work with relevant government ministries and agencies to explore and establish shock-absorbers to the prevailing aid cut.
The decision from plenary was triggered by a joint communication submitted by Senators Amara Konneh (Gbarpolu), Gbezohngar Findley (Grand Bassa), Abraham Darius Dillon (Montserrado), and Augustine Chea (Sinoe), who collectively emphasized the urgent need for the Liberian government to reassess its budgeting and to develop financing strategies due to the possible disruption of USAID-funded initiatives.
Founded in 1961 by President John F. Kennedy, USAID has played an essential role in global development, and its impact in Liberia is far-reaching, affecting sectors such as health, education, and governance among other key sector areas.
The Trump administration’s shift in foreign aid policy has raised alarms, particularly with the agency’s cancellation and or freeze of all projects worldwide for a period of 90 days, citing the need to realign USAID’s efforts with the “America First” agenda.
With such policy, members of the Liberian Senate led by Pro Tempore Nyounblee Karnga Lawrence, has been seeking possible solution for a way forward for the common good of Liberia.
The hearings, chaired by Grand Cape Mount County Senator Debah Varpilah who also chairs the Senate health committees, were used to ask the Finance Ministry in particular to provide a full detailed analysis report that will inform the Senate on the next course of action.
The Ministries of Education and Health have also been cited to return and provide more information on the situation. Health Minister proper, not deputies, is asked to form part of the hearing.

a5773.t:
Kairo (UNA/WAFA) – Die Arabische Liga erneuerte ihren Aufruf, das palästinensische Volk vor Völkermord, Vertreibung und ethnischer Säuberung zu schützen und die Liquidierung seiner zentralen Sache zu verhindern. Grundlage hierfür sind Resolutionen zur internationalen Legitimität, das Völkerrecht und einschlägige Abkommen, darunter die Resolutionen 904 (1994) und 605 (1987) des Sicherheitsrats, die Resolution 20/10 (2018) der Generalversammlung und der Vertrag über gemeinsame Verteidigungs- und Wirtschaftskooperation zwischen den Mitgliedsstaaten der Arabischen Liga. Dabei wird der Schutz der Interessen der Mitgliedsstaaten, ihrer souveränen Entscheidungen und ihrer rechtlichen Verpflichtungen gewährleistet.
Dies geschah zum Abschluss der außerordentlichen Sitzung des Völkerbundrates auf Delegiertenebene, die am heutigen Sonntag im Hauptsitz des Völkerbundes in Kairo unter jordanischem Vorsitz und auf Ersuchen des Staates Palästina unter Beteiligung aller arabischen Länder stattfand. Auf der Sitzung wurden Mechanismen für arabische und internationale Maßnahmen erörtert, um dem von der Besatzungsmacht Israel begangenen Völkermord am palästinensischen Volk ein Ende zu setzen. Dazu gehören auch die Pläne zur vollständigen militärischen Kontrolle des Gazastreifens und zur Umsetzung des Plans zur Zwangsumsiedlung im Kontext der seit 673 Tagen andauernden Verbrechen der Aggression, der Belagerung und des systematischen Hungers.
Der Rat verurteilte die Entscheidungen und Pläne der israelischen Regierung, die Besetzung des Gazastreifens fortzusetzen und die Bevölkerung zu vertreiben. Er betrachtete sie als Verstoß gegen das Völkerrecht, als eklatante Aggression gegen die nationale Sicherheit und Interessen der arabischen Länder und als Bedrohung für Frieden und Stabilität in der Region. Er betonte zudem die Notwendigkeit, die Beschlüsse der gemeinsamen arabischen und arabisch-islamischen Gipfeltreffen umzusetzen, um die israelische Blockade des Gazastreifens zu durchbrechen und die Einreise humanitärer Hilfe auf dem Land-, See- und Luftweg in Zusammenarbeit mit den Vereinten Nationen und ihren Organisationen, einschließlich des UNRWA, zu erzwingen.
Der Rat forderte die beiden arabischen Mitglieder des Sicherheitsrats (Algerien und Somalia) und die Arabische Gruppe in New York auf, ihre Bemühungen zur Beendigung der israelischen Aggression fortzusetzen. Dazu gehört auch die Vorlage eines Resolutionsentwurfs gemäß Kapitel VII, der die Besatzungsmacht zu einer Feuereinstellung verpflichten, die Einfuhr von Hilfsgütern erlauben und die Besatzung beenden soll. Außerdem sollen internationale Sanktionen gegen sie verhängt werden. Außerdem sollen die Staaten aufgefordert werden, rechtliche und administrative Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, darunter die Verhinderung des Exports, der Weitergabe oder des Transits von Waffen, Munition und militärischem Material nach Israel, die Überprüfung der Wirtschaftsbeziehungen mit Israel sowie die Einleitung von Ermittlungen und Strafverfolgungen gegen israelische Beamte.
Er forderte die Zivilgesellschaft und Menschenrechtsorganisationen auf, die an israelischen Kriegsverbrechen Beteiligten aufzuspüren und zur Rechenschaft zu ziehen.
Er betonte die Ermächtigung des Staates Palästina, im Rahmen des politischen Programms der Palästinensischen Befreiungsorganisation die volle Regierungsverantwortung im Gazastreifen und im Westjordanland, einschließlich Ostjerusalem, zu übernehmen.
Der Rat verurteilte Israels Einsatz von Hunger als Mittel des Völkermords. 200 palästinensische Zivilisten, die Hälfte davon Kinder, starben dabei. Auch die von den Besatzungstruppen unter dem Deckmantel der sogenannten „Gaza Humanitarian Foundation“ aufgestellten „Todesfallen“ forderten 1500 Märtyrer und Tausende Verletzte. Der Rat machte Israel für die Blockade und ihre Folgen voll verantwortlich.
Er betonte außerdem den Boykott von Unternehmen, die zur Stärkung der Besatzungswirtschaft beitragen oder die Verbrechen des Völkermords und der ethnischen Säuberung unterstützen, insbesondere jene, die in den Berichten des Menschenrechtsrats und des UN-Sonderberichterstatters erwähnt werden. Er bekräftigte die Umsetzung der Resolutionen 2735, 2712 und 2720 des Sicherheitsrats bezüglich des Waffenstillstands, der Rückkehr der Vertriebenen, der Verteilung von Hilfsgütern, des Gefangenenaustauschs und des vollständigen Rückzugs aus dem Gazastreifen.
Der Rat begrüßte die internationalen Positionen, die die israelische Militärkontrolle über Gaza und die Annexion des Westjordanlands ablehnen. Er bestätigte die Fortsetzung der Ratssitzung und beauftragte den Generalsekretär, die Umsetzung der Resolutionen zu überwachen und der nächsten Sitzung einen Bericht vorzulegen.
Der palästinensische Delegierte in der Liga, Botschafter Muhannad Al-Aklouk, betonte seinerseits, wie wichtig es sei, die internationalen Bemühungen fortzusetzen und zu intensivieren, um den Vernichtungs- und Hungerkrieg gegen das palästinensische Volk zu beenden und die Pläne der Besatzungsmacht zu vereiteln, Gaza unter ihre Kontrolle zu bringen und das Westjordanland zu annektieren. Er erklärte, der Rat habe dem palästinensischen Resolutionsentwurf zur Beendigung des Krieges und zur sofortigen Lieferung von Hilfsgütern einstimmig zugestimmt und betonte: „Israel metzelt die Menschheit der Welt nieder, und Palästina ist der Schauplatz dieses Verbrechens.“
Al-Aklouk wies darauf hin, dass die Besatzungsmacht mehr als eine Viertelmillion Palästinenser getötet und verletzt habe, darunter 18,500 Kinder, und über 200 Zivilisten verhungern ließ, die Hälfte davon Kinder. Er fügte hinzu, dass die Pläne der Besatzungsmacht darauf abzielen, die Nakba von 1948 durch neue Zwangsumsiedlungen zu wiederholen, da das israelische Parlament der Annexion des besetzten Westjordanlands zugestimmt und die Gründung eines palästinensischen Staates dort verhindert habe.
(Enden)
a5773.en:
Cairo (UNA/WAFA) – The Arab League renewed its call to protect the Palestinian people from genocide, displacement and ethnic cleansing and to prevent the liquidation of its central cause. The basis for this is resolutions of international legitimacy, international law and relevant agreements, including Security Council resolutions 904 (1994) and 605 (1987), General Assembly resolution 20/10 (2018) and the Treaty of Joint Defence and Economic Cooperation between the member states of the Arab League. In doing so, the protection of the interests of the member states, their sovereign decisions and their legal obligations is guaranteed.

This took place at the conclusion of the extraordinary session of the League Council at the level of delegates, which was held today, Sunday, at the League’s headquarters in Cairo under Jordanian chairmanship and at the request of the State of Palestine, with the participation of all Arab countries. At the session, mechanisms for Arab and international measures were discussed in order to put an end to the genocide committed by the occupying power Israel against the Palestinian people. These also include the plans for complete military control of the Gaza Strip and for implementing the plan for forced resettlement in the context of the crimes of aggression, siege and systematic starvation that have been ongoing for 673 days.

The Council condemned the decisions and plans of the Israeli government to continue the occupation of the Gaza Strip and to displace the population. It considered them a violation of international law, a flagrant aggression against the national security and interests of the Arab countries and a threat to peace and stability in the region. It also stressed the need to implement the decisions of the joint Arab and Arab-Islamic summits in order to break the Israeli blockade of the Gaza Strip and to force the entry of humanitarian aid by land, sea and air in cooperation with the United Nations and its organisations, including UNRWA.

The Council called on the two Arab members of the Security Council (Algeria and Somalia) and the Arab Group in New York to continue their efforts to end the Israeli aggression. This also includes the submission of a draft resolution under Chapter VII that would oblige the occupying power to a ceasefire, allow the import of aid supplies and end the occupation. In addition, international sanctions are to be imposed on it. States are also to be called upon to take legal and administrative measures, including preventing the export, transfer or transit of weapons, ammunition and military material to Israel, reviewing economic relations with Israel, and initiating investigations and criminal prosecutions against Israeli officials.

It called on civil society and human rights organisations to track down and hold accountable those involved in Israeli war crimes.

It emphasised the empowerment of the State of Palestine to assume full governmental responsibility in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, within the framework of the political programme of the Palestine Liberation Organisation.

The Council condemned Israel’s use of starvation as a means of genocide. Two hundred Palestinian civilians, half of them children, died as a result. The “death traps” set up by the occupation forces under the cover of the so-called “Gaza Humanitarian Foundation” also claimed 1,500 martyrs and thousands of wounded. The Council held Israel fully responsible for the blockade and its consequences.

It also stressed the boycott of companies that contribute to strengthening the occupation economy or that support the crimes of genocide and ethnic cleansing, in particular those mentioned in the reports of the Human Rights Council and the UN Special Rapporteur. It reaffirmed the implementation of Security Council resolutions 2735, 2712 and 2720 concerning the ceasefire, the return of the displaced, the distribution of aid supplies, the exchange of prisoners and the complete withdrawal from the Gaza Strip.

The Council welcomed the international positions that reject Israeli military control over Gaza and the annexation of the West Bank. It confirmed the continuation of the Council session and instructed the Secretary-General to monitor the implementation of the resolutions and to submit a report to the next session.

For his part, the Palestinian delegate to the League, Ambassador Muhannad Al-Aklouk, stressed how important it is to continue and intensify international efforts in order to end the war of extermination and starvation against the Palestinian people and to thwart the occupying power’s plans to bring Gaza under its control and to annex the West Bank. He stated that the Council had unanimously agreed to the Palestinian draft resolution on ending the war and on the immediate delivery of aid supplies, and stressed: “Israel is slaughtering the humanity of the world, and Palestine is the scene of this crime.”

Al-Aklouk pointed out that the occupying power had killed and injured more than a quarter of a million Palestinians, including 18,500 children, and had let more than 200 civilians starve to death, half of them children. He added that the occupying power’s plans aim to repeat the Nakba of 1948 through new forced resettlements, since the Israeli parliament had approved the annexation of the occupied West Bank and prevented the establishment of a Palestinian state there.

(Ends)

a6044.t:
The number of pretrial detainees in various prisons across the country only paints a gloomy picture of the country’s justice system.
By Lincoln G. Peters
Monrovia, October 2, 2024/At least 71% of inmates languishing behind bars in Liberia are said to be pretrial detainees, according to Liberian National Bar Association (LNBA) President Cllr. Sylvester D. Rennie.
“Even those who commit non-bailable crimes are also incarcerated. It has been observed that most of these detainees at our various prison facilities in Liberia are pre-trial detainees, which constitute 71% of the overall number of detainees in the Country,” said Cllr. Rennie.
Cllr. Rennie made this disclosure over the weekend when his organization (LNBA) launched the final report of the LNBA-National Election Commission Electoral Support Project and the Legal Aid Promoting Access to Justice Project.
However, he said when these offenders are arrested and taken to the law, in most instances, they are unable to meet the needed provisions to secure their release and are therefore incarcerated.
LNBA, in collaboration with the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) and with funding from the International Narcotics and Law Enforcement, has also launched a pre-trial detainees project to address the over 71% pre-trial deletion in Liberia.
The overall purpose of the project is to reduce the number of pretrial detainees in Montserrado County and improve access to justice for all Liberians and provide Legal Aid Service for Egregious Cases and pre-trial detainees.
The implementation period for this project is one year, from 15 July 2024 to 14 July 2025.
The project was officially launched in the Temple of Justice Conference Room and was graced by the Chief Justice and Associate Justices of Liberia, Liberia’s Minister of Justice, among others.
The diplomatic community was represented by United States Ambassador Mark C. Toner and Mr. Anthony Ohemeng-Boamah, Resident Representative of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), among others.
Giving an overview of what promoted the program’s implementation and partnership, LNBA President Cllr. Rennie said the LNBA has realized that crimes are committed daily, violating the law.
“As a means of having some of our prisons decongested, the LNBA and the UNDP with funding from the International Narcotics & Law Enforcement (INL) signed a grant agreement for the decongestion of pretrial detainees at the Monrovia Central Prison. This process is for one year, and it is also being launched. We want to thank the UNDP and the INL for this collaboration.” Cllr. Rennie stated.
Providing the project’s goal and objectives, Cllr. Frederick L. M. Gbemie, Project Manager, said that the project’s goal is to sensitize, encourage, and promote legal protection for vulnerable and indigent citizens through the provision of pro bono legal aid services for the most egregious cases by members of the LNBA as an alternate condition for renewal of practicing licenses.
He further indicated that by this intervention, the LNBA seeks to sensitize and encourage members of the LNBA to provide pro bono legal aid as one of the alternate conditions for the renewal of practicing licenses:
” The LNBA will Provide legal aid services for the most egregious cases to reduce docket overcrowding and pre-trial detention in Montserrado county and educate citizens on how to access the LNBA Pro Bono Legal Aid Services and encourage indigents to take advantage of the opportunity to access justice. To successfully make the above intervention, the LNBA Action would be to hold one day of LNBA stakeholders’ clarity and brainstorming meetings,” he added.
The Liberian legal luminary stated that the launch of the project holds a one-day LNBA Legal Aid National Symposium, produce and publicize Pro-Bono/ Free Legal Aid Service awareness materials such as drama, jingles, and stickers for pro bono legal aid service awareness. -Edited by Othello B. Garblah

Through the funding, Comprehensive HIV Prevention and Care Programme will be implemented by Jhpiego, Stepping Stones International, and Tebelopele Wellness Centre over a two-year period in 18 districts across the country. It also aims to improve health outcomes through strengthened primary health care and social services. During the programme launch this week, Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health (MoH) Prof Oatlhokwa Nkomazana said the projects were carefully designed to provide complementary support to the government’s critical priorities in the areas of orphans and vulnerable children (OVC).
She added that their collective goal was to end HIV as a public health threat by 2030 by demonstrating global best practices in health and revitalising primary health care in the country. “The Ministry congratulates the three organisations; Stepping Stones International, Tebelopele Wellness Centre and Jhpiego on being selected to implement these transformative programmes to strengthen our HIV response as a country. We sincerely appreciate the U.S. government’s unwavering dedication to supporting Botswana's health initiatives,” she said. “Our government has made significant strides in the global HIV response, being a global leader in the fight against HIV/AIDS. Today, the country has one of the highest rates of viral suppression in the world and has achieved the UNAIDS 2030 fast-track targets of 95-95-95 by reaching an impressive 95-98-98.” Nkomazana further stated that despite that monumental achievement, their work was by no means over adding that they had a collective responsibility to reach all populations and leaving no one behind, especially the remaining 5-2-2 populations. She also said they had to continue to innovate and expand their services to address those gaps. She added that their focus must be on elevating the quality of life for all and sustaining the gains by maintaining a country-owned, sustainable direction that leaves no one behind.
